10.8.3 Interface protection for wind turbines connected to distribution networks

Section 10.8.1 considered the protection of the wind turbines from the effects of insulation failure and subsequent high fault currents, which were supplied by the distribution network. However, protection is also required to ensure that a wind farm does not feed into faults on the distribution network or attempt to supply an isolated section of network.

The problem is illustrated in Figure 10.21. For faults on the network, the difficulty is that wind turbines are not a reliable source of fault current and so circuit breaker B may not be opened by over-current protection. Thus, for the fault shown the current operated protection on the network is used to open circuit breaker A. This then isolates the wind turbine which begins to speed up as the wind input remains but it is no longer possible to export power to the network. In fact, this acceleration begins as soon as the fault occurs, and before circuit breaker A trips, as the fault depresses the network voltage and so restricts the export of power. Circuit breaker B is then opened by over-frequency relays which detect the increase in rotational speed of the wind turbine, and hence the increase in frequency of the output, or by under/over-voltage relays which detect that the connection to the network has been lost by monitoring the change in voltage. It is common for the over/under frequency and voltage relays to be time delayed by, for example 500 milliseconds, to reduce spurious operation. Hence in high winds it is possible that the wind turbine will shut down on mechanical over speed protection which is set to limit the speed of the aerodynamic rotor.

This sequential tripping using voltage and frequency sensitive relays which operate once the generator has been isolated is not generally considered to be good practice in the protection of conventional power systems. However, with the use of induction generators or voltage source converters there is little option and so the arrangement is generally accepted for wind farms.

The issue of islanding is the possibility that the output of the wind turbine (in terms of both real and reactive power) matches precisely the local load. In this case even though circuit breaker A opens there will be no change in the voltage or frequency of the wind turbine and so circuit breaker B will not operate. Most distribution utilities are extremely sensitive to possible islanded operation for a number of reasons:

  • The possibility that customers may receive supply outside the required limits of frequency and voltage.

  • The possibility that part of the network may be operated without adequate neutral earths.

  • The danger associated with out-of-phase reclosing.

  • That it is against the regulations governing operation of the distribution network.

  • The potential danger to staff operating the distribution network.

From the point of view of the wind farm operator the main danger is in out-of-phase reclosing. Many distribution circuits have automatic reclosing to allow transient faults, particularly on overhead lines, to be cleared without prolonged interruption to customers. Thus, circuit breaker A may be arranged to reclose up to a few seconds after opening. If the circuit breaker B is still closed then very high currents and torques will occur as the network voltage is applied out-of-phase to the wind turbine. This is the main technical driver for fast islanding protection as, particularly with wind turbines, it is very unlikely that the required matching of generator output (both real and reactive power) to the load will be sustained for any length of time.

Considerable efforts have been made to devise robust protection systems to detect islanding. However, it may be seen to be very difficult as, by the principal of superposition, if there is no current flowing in circuit breaker A then it makes no difference to the network conditions at the wind turbine whether it is open or closed. The commonly used relays are the so-called rocof (rate of change of frequency) devices or vector-shift relays which measure the jump in the voltage vector when islanding occurs. Both relays rely on some current (and hence real power) flowing in circuit breaker A and can be adjusted to varying levels of sensitivity. However, if they are set too sensitive then they tend to be prone to spurious nuisance tripping due to external disturbances on the power system (e.g. the tripping of a large remote conventional power plant).

A further complication occurs if the fault shown in Figure 10.22 is not between phases but is between a single phase and ground. Faults of this type are particularly common on overhead lines. It can be seen that the turbine transformer (e.g. \({33}/{0.69}\mathrm{{kV}}\) ) has a Delta winding on the High Voltage side. This has no accessible neutral point and no connection to ground is made. Thus, there is no path in which the ground current may flow and so, in principal, the single-phase earth fault will remain indefinitely with no current flowing. In practice some stray capacitive currents will flow but these will not be enough to operate conventional earth fault protection and will, in fact, lead to intermittent arcing. The conventional solution is to use a neutral voltage displacement relay to detect that one phase of the circuit is connected to ground and so the neutral is displaced. The disadvantage of this scheme is its cost as a complex (five limb) voltage transformer is required on the high voltage circuit. Although this can be accommodated for a large wind farm the expense is sometimes difficult to justify for individual wind turbines.

The requirements for interface protection vary widely between different countries. Some countries favour the use of transfer tripping whereby when any upstream utility circuit breaker is opened this action is communicated to the wind farm circuit breaker which is then immediately opened. Although this provides a guarantee against islanded operation it can be expensive to implement as communication channels from a number of remote circuit breakers are required. It is interesting to note that in Holland, where almost all the distribution system is underground and so auto-reclose is not used, there is no requirement for loss-of-mains protection. In Denmark, positive phase sequence under-voltage relays are used extensively and appear to be effective in detecting islanded operation. No doubt over time practices will converge but, at present, very considerable national differences remain.

10.9 Distributed generation and the Grid Codes

Wind turbines are connected individually and in small groups to the medium voltage distribution network or in large wind farms to the high voltage distribution and transmission network. The connection rules and performance required by the power system operator depend on the size of the wind farms and the voltage of the network to which they are connected.

Individual wind turbines and small wind farms connected to the distribution network come under regulations such as G59/1 in the UK, for generators up to 5 MW and 20 kV, (Electricity Network Association, 1991) and IEEE 1547, for groups of generators up to 10 MVA, in the USA (IEEE, 2003). The philosophy of these regulations is that the wind generation is too small to have any significant impact on the frequency of the main power system. Thus, these regulations require that the wind turbines disconnect if there is any disturbance in the power system or if a section of the network becomes islanded. When the network voltage or frequency is outside the normal operating range the turbines are tripped and not reconnected until normal network conditions are restored. Sensitive loss of mains protection is used to detect islanding.

The thrust of these regulations reflects the concerns of the distribution network operators to avoid islanded operation and to ensure there is no possibility of out of phase re-closure, back feeding sections of the network with the possible safety hazards or operating an ungrounded system. The stability of the power system is provided by the large central generators and all wind turbines falling under these regulations must operate with power factor control taking their voltage from the network. There is no requirement for real power control and the wind turbines make no contribution to maintaining system frequency.

In contrast, larger wind farms fall under a different set of regulations, known as the Grid Codes. These requirements are imposed by the transmission system operators and reflect their concern that larger wind farms have a significant effect on the main power system. Here the philosophy is that rather than disconnect if the voltage and frequency of the power system are outside their normal limits, perhaps because of a system fault or loss of a large generator, the wind farms should stay connected to support the power system. In addition the wind farms are required to have the facility to control their terminal voltage and to be able to provide frequency support. These wind farms are considered large enough to influence the transmission system voltage through their output of reactive power and the network frequency by their generation of real power.

The size of wind farm and voltage level at which these two rather different approaches change reflects the relative significance of wind generation compared to the size of the conventional generation system. Thus, the GB Grid Code applies to wind farms above 50 MW in England but 10 MW in parts of Scotland. In the USA, Texas with its large wind farms has a well developed transmission Grid Code while some other states with limited wind energy at present do not. As wind energy continues to increase, it is likely that versions of the Grid Codes will apply to smaller wind farms to ensure they contribute to the operation of the power system. However, operating practice of distribution networks will then have to be revised.

Many countries have their own national standards for the connection of small distributed generation and their own Grid Codes for large wind farms. These are continually evolving as the importance of wind generation and other forms of distributed generation increase and efforts are continuing to harmonise these regulations. The principles of these documents are discussed with examples that are illustrative only.

10.9.1 Grid Code - continuous operation

The Grid Codes follow from similar requirements that apply to the connection of large fossil and hydro central generators. Thus, they do not address individual wind turbines in a wind farm but only the performance of the entire farm at the point it is connected to the transmission network.

Large wind farms are required to be able to operate continuously over the range of frequency and voltage that might be expected on the power system and not to trip during system disturbances. This is to ensure that they continue to provide energy into the power system when the transmission network voltage and frequencies are disturbed. Figure 10.22 shows the typical of the requirements for large wind farms connected to High Voltage networks. The precise values of frequency and voltage vary country by country. There have been recorded examples in both Britain and mainland Europe of a major system frequency drop, caused by the simultaneous loss of central generators or circuits, being made worse by the tripping of distributed generators that were protected against islanded operation by sensitive frequency, voltage or rate of change of frequency relays. Continuous operation over a range of frequencies and voltages ensures that large wind farms contribute to the stability of the power system.

10.9.2 Grid Code - voltage and power factor control

The voltages of a transmission network are determined mainly by the flows of reactive power. Large wind farms are required to be able to operate either by controlling their terminal voltage or exchanging a defined level of reactive power with the transmission network. A typical requirement is shown in Figure 10.23. The wind farm is required to be able to operate anywhere within this area as instructed by the transmission system operator.

Figure 10.23 Grid Code - voltage and power factor control. Typical reactive power requirement of a grid connected wind farm (National Grid, 2008). Point A is equivalent (in MVAr) to: 0.95 leading Power Factor at Rated MW output; point B is equivalent (in MVAr) to: 0.95 lagging Power Factor at Rated MW output; point C is equivalent (in MVAr) to: -5% of Rated MW output; point D is equivalent (in MVAr) to: +5% of Rated MW output; point E is equivalent (in MVAr) to: -12% of Rated MW output.

Variable speed wind turbines can, in principle, operate at any power factor within the rating of their power electronic equipment. In practice it is difficult to ensure rapid compliance with the requirements for the reactive power output of a large wind farm because of the:

  • Difficulty of rapidly coordinating the reactive power generation of a large number of geographically dispersed wind turbines.

  • Reactive power drawn by the wind farm transformers which varies with both real and reactive power transmitted.

  • Increase in costs of the wind turbines if a large reactive power range is specified.

Hence it is common for additional reactive power compensation equipment (e.g. a STATCOM) to be installed at the point of connection of the wind farm to the network to assist in meeting this Grid Code requirement.

10.9.3 Grid Code - frequency response

The frequency of a power system is determined by the instantaneous balance of real power generation and load. If the load exceeds the generation the frequency will drop and if there is an excess of generation the frequency will rise. The rate of change of frequency is determined by the spinning inertia of all generators and spinning loads connected to the power system.

Figure 10.24 Grid Code - frequency response: high frequency response black line, de-loaded turbine grey line

Thus, if the frequency of the power system increases, perhaps because a large load is disconnected, the wind turbines must reduce their real power output (Figure 10.24).

In order to provide low frequency response the wind turbines must be de-loaded either by adjusting their blade pitch angles or by operating at off-optimal rotational speed. Several approaches to active power control including delta control and gradient power control are discussed in Wind Energy - The Facts (European Wind Energy Association, 2009). The requirement for de-loaded operation is specified in many of the Grid Codes but is rarely called on by the power system operator as it results in wind energy being wasted.

10.9.4 Grid Code - fault ride through

Short-circuit faults on the transmission network cause the voltage to be depressed over a wide area. Faults are inevitable in any power system, for example due to lightning, and the voltage depressions may extend for hundreds of kilometres. Circuit breakers will clear transmission faults in approximately 100 milliseconds by isolating the faulted section of network and the network voltage then recovers but faults on the lower voltage networks take longer to clear.

A network fault may result in the isolation of a circuit and loss of central generation and it is just at this time that the wind farms should continue to provide energy into the power system. The wind farms should remain stable and connected during any network disturbance and so are required to exhibit an ability to ride through voltage depressions caused by short-circuit faults.

The power that any generator can export is the product of voltage and current and so if its terminal voltage is depressed the generator cannot export its power to the network and will over-speed. The mechanical energy is stored as rotational kinetic energy in the generator and its prime mover. When a fixed speed induction generator wind turbine over-speeds due to a network fault and the voltage is restored it will draw large amounts of reactive power which results in a further voltage depression and possible voltage instability.

A variable speed wind turbine is better able to ride through voltage depressions and a transient reduction in output power by allowing the rotor speed to increase. However, a robust control system is needed to ensure that the converters remain synchronized with the network during the voltage depression.

Figure 10.25 shows the voltage time envelope within which a wind farm must continue to operate. The wind farm must withstand a drop to zero volts for 140 milliseconds and a reduction to \({80}\%\) volts for 1.2 seconds. An example of a voltage depression caused by a fault is also shown. In this example, the fault is cleared within \({385}\mathrm{\;{ms}}\) and the wind farm continues to operate through this network fault.

10.9.5 Synthetic inertia

The conventional control system of a variable speed wind turbine does not consider the power system frequency. The frequency is used to synchronize the switching of the power electronics of the network side converter but the main control loop measures the rotational speed of the generator and applies a torque so that the wind turbine follows its pre-determined operating characteristic (Figures 6.18 and 6.19). Thus, in the event of a drop in power system frequency, caused, for example by the sudden disconnection of a large central generator, a variable speed wind turbine will not provide any additional energy as the system frequency falls. This is in contrast to a conventional synchronous generator, or a fixed speed induction generator, that will transfer some of its kinetic energy to the power system as the frequency and the speed of rotation of the generator falls.

This lack of response of variable speed wind turbines to a drop in system frequency can be overcome by adding additional control loops as shown in Figure 10.26. The inertia is synthesized by measuring the rate of change of system frequency. The magnitude of the frequency drop may also be used to apply additional torque to the rotor, slow it down and so transfer kinetic energy to the network.

The provision of synthetic inertia is required by some, but not all Grid Codes.

10.10 Wind energy and the generation system

Throughout the world, most electricity is generated using large synchronous electrical machines (up to 1000 MW capacity) driven by turbines from fossil, hydro or nuclear energy. Until a few years ago, the amount of wind energy being generated was so small that it acted merely to reduce the electrical load seen by these generators and had no significant impact on either the planning or operation of the generation system. This is now changing rapidly with wind energy becoming significant both for the development (planning) of the generation system and its operation.

Figure 10.26 Additional control loops to provide synthetic inertia to a variable speed wind turbine \({T}_{sp}\) is the set point of the torque controller of the power electronic converters. (Anaya-Lara, 2009)

In many countries, the electricity system has been liberalized and separated into companies dealing with generation, energy retail, transmission and distribution. Some parts of a liberalized electricity system operate as a market (generation and energy retail) while others are natural monopolies (transmission and distribution) and are regulated by the state for the benefit of customers. Although the market influences the way generators and energy retailers behave in the short term the underlying operation of the electrical power system remains unchanged and the market and regulation can be considered as merely mechanisms to discover the most efficient way for the various actors to behave.

10.10.1 Capacity credit

All generating systems (and indeed all aspects of the power system) are designed assuming a probability of failure. All pieces of plant (e.g. generators, transformers, overhead lines and cables) have a finite probability of failure and any design for a completely reliable system would be infinitely expensive. Traditionally the probability that load would exceed the available generation has been defined in terms of generation adequacy. Before liberalisation, the England and Wales generating system was designed to a Loss of Load Probability (LOLP) of 0.09 . This meant electrical demand was expected to exceed available generation on average nine times a century. A LOLP of 0.09 with the mainly coal generating system of England and Wales in the 1980s required a generation planning margin of \({24}\%\) (i.e. the generating capacity built would exceed the peak load by 24%). The French system was designed to a Loss of Load Expectation (LOLE) of three hours per year while the Eire system assumed demand would exceed generation for eight hours per year. In North America a LOLP of 0.1 or LOLE of 2.4 hours/year were common. Similar criteria were used by other major generating utilities.

This principle of planning for a defined level of adequacy is illustrated in Figure 10.27 where the probability distributions of the load and generation are shown. The risk of insufficient generation is shown by the intersection of these probability distributions. All generators have a probability of not being available due to breakdown but wind generation has a higher probability of not generating than fossil generation as it may not generate because of low wind speeds as well as equipment failure. Thus, adding wind energy to the generation portfolio has the effect of widening the probability distribution of generation and, hence, increasing the generation planning margin.

Figure 10.27 Generation adequacy. (Jenkins, Ekanayake and Strbac, 2010)

Calculations to establish the contribution of wind energy to generation adequacy of a power system are undertaken in a similar manner to those for fossil generators (Billinton and Allan, 1996) except that rather than consider only one of two states of a conventional generator (available or not available) wind generators are represented by a number of states to reflect the probability of generation at various wind speeds. These states and their associated probabilities are used to construct a Capacity Outage Probability Table and so calculate the probability of generation being available. As the wind generation is added, conventional generation is removed until the same adequacy is achieved. This approach then allows the capacity value of wind energy to be calculated.

The capacity value of wind generation is described by its capacity credit (Milligan and Parsons, 1999) which is defined as the reduction in the requirement for capacity of conventional plant, made possible by the introduction of wind energy, while maintaining reliable supplies of electricity. The capacity reduction of conventional generation is expressed as percentage of the wind generating capacity in the system. In summary, the capacity credit of wind is assessed through quantification of the generation adequacy of the generation system with and without wind power under a standard reliability criterion (e.g. LOLP or LOLE).

Figure 10.28 shows how the capacity credit of wind energy varies with the penetration of wind energy on the Great Britain power system. It may be seen that at low penetrations the capacity credit is close to the wind energy capacity factors and then reduces with increasing penetration. The benefit of geographical diversity is shown clearly with geographically diverse wind farms giving a higher capacity credit than if they are all located in the same area.

10.10.2 Wind power forecasting

The electrical power system is operated by balancing supply and demand on a second-by-second basis. Thus, as well an appropriate capacity of generation being constructed it needs to be operated to meet the load. This is known traditionally as Unit Commitment and is the selection of the optimum (minimum cost or minimum emission) choice of generators to meet the load within constraints. The constraints include the generator operational constraints (e.g. minimum up and down times of thermal generators), network constraints (e.g. loading of circuits) and the requirement to maintain adequate reserves (e.g. partially loaded spinning generators). Once the generators to be connected to the network are selected, their most economic output is determined through Economic Despatch. Unit Commitment and Economic Despatch together are often referred to as generation scheduling.

Figure 10.28 The capacity credit of wind generation versus the level of wind penetration in the Great Britain electricity system. (Jenkins, Ekanayake and Strbac, 2010)

In a traditional vertically integrated electricity system, the scheduling of the generation system was optimised centrally by the system operator. In a market based system each generating company will optimise their own portfolio of generators with the objective of meeting the contracts they have struck with energy retailers. However, the principles of having to commit plant, often up to eight hours in advance for large thermal generators, and then optimise its operation remains.

The objective is always to meet the demand at minimum cost (or emissions) and so knowledge of the demand is critical. If historic demand and factors such as ambient temperature and TV programs are taken into account it is possible to forecast electrical load demand with considerable accuracy (typically within 3%). However, the introduction of large quantities of wind energy into the power system significantly increases uncertainty of the level of residual load that will be needed by other generations. Hence, forecasting of wind power output becomes extremely important for power system operation (Boyle, 2009).

Figure 10.29 Flows of information in a wind power forecasting system. (After, Fox et al., 2007)

Effective forecasting of wind power output is required for:

  • The scheduling of generators and balancing supply and demand.

  • Determining the reserve generation needed, either part-loaded generators or fast-start gas turbines. This requires a prediction of the accuracy of the forecast.

  • Effective operation of the transmission system and managing congestion on circuits.

Forecasts of up to four to six hours ahead may be based on measured data (wind speeds or wind farm power output) using analysis of the previous time series. A large number of techniques have been investigated and modest improvements over persistence can be achieved. The persistence model assumes that the forecast is the same as the last measured value.

All predictions with a longer time horizon are based on Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) using weather forecasts. Global NWP models are operated by a number of national weather services. They use meteorological observations from weather stations and satellites together with a numerical model to predict the future state of the earth's atmosphere. They are very computationally intensive and so use a rather coarse spatial mesh. Local area NWP models take as their input the results of the global model to provide higher resolution but over only a part of the earth. These local forecasts, which may be purchased from the national weather service, are used as an input of the wind power forecasting model (Figure 10.29).

The wind speed forecasts from the local NWP model are provided on a grid perhaps \({20}\mathrm{\;{km}}\) square, every eight hours over a 48-hour time horizon. These are then translated (downscaled) to the wind farm site at the height of the turbines. In flat terrain this may be done by spatial interpolation but in more complex terrain a meso-scale model is used. Using this site wind speed, the wind farm output is then modelled taking into account local topography and loss of energy in wind turbine wakes. Model Output Statistics (MOS) are then used to refine the model by comparing its outputs with measurements from the wind farms of power output and wind speeds.

Appendix A10 Simple calculations for the connection of wind turbines

A10.1 The Per-unit system

The per unit system (Weedy and Cory, 1998) is simply a technique used by electrical power engineers to simplify calculation by expressing all values as a ratio of:

  • actual value (in any unit);

  • base or reference value (in the same unit).

Its advantages include: (1) a reduction in the appearance of \(\sqrt{}3\) in the calculations (2) that similar per unit values apply to systems of various sizes and (3) by appropriate choice of voltage bases the solution of networks containing several transformers is facilitated.

For simple calculations, such as those required for assessment of a wind turbine or small wind farm on a simple distribution circuit, all that is required is to:

  1. Assume an arbitrary base VA (e.g. 10 MVA for a small wind farm connection).

  2. Select voltage bases of each voltage level of the network (e.g. \({33}\mathrm{{kV}}\) and \({11}\mathrm{{kV}}\) ). These voltage bases should be related by the nominal turns ratios of the transformers.

  3. Calculate the appropriate real and reactive power flows at the generator terminals in per unit (i.e. for a Power flow of \(5\mathrm{{MW}}\) with the base VA chosen as \({10}\mathrm{{MVA}}\) , the per unit value is \(P = 5/{10}\) or 0.5 per unit. Similarly for a Reactive Power flow of \(1\mathrm{{MVA}}r\) the per unit value is \(Q = 1/{10}\) or 0.1 per unit).

  4. If necessary transform the impedances of the circuit from ohmic to per unit values using a base impedance of \({Z}_{\text{ base }} = {V}^{2}{}_{\text{ base }}/V{A}_{\text{ base }}\) .

  5. The base current at any particular voltage level is calculated from: \({I}_{\text{ base }} = V{A}_{\text{ base }}/ \; \sqrt{}3 \times {V}_{\text{ base }}\) .

A10.2 Power flows, slow voltage variations and network losses

If the output from a distributed wind turbine generator is absorbed locally by an adjacent load then the effect on the distribution network voltage and losses is likely to be beneficial. However, if it is necessary to transport the power through the distribution network then increased losses may occur and slow voltage variations may become excessive (Jenkins, Ekanayake and Strbac, 2010).

If the wind generator operates at unity power factor (i.e. Reactive Power \(Q = 0\) ), then the voltage rise in a lightly loaded radial circuit (Figure A10.1) is given approximately by:

\[ {\Delta V} = {V}_{1} - {V}_{0} = {PR}/{V}_{0} \tag{A10.1} \]

Operating the generator at a leading power factor (absorbing reactive power) acts to reduce the voltage rise but at the expense of increased network losses. In this case the voltage rise is given by:

\[ {\Delta V} = {V}_{1} - {V}_{0} = \left( {{PR} - {XQ}}\right) /{V}_{0} \tag{A10.2} \]

Figure A10.1 Fixed-speed wind turbine on a radial circuit

The impedance of an overhead \({11}\mathrm{{kV}}\) distribution circuit may, typically, have a ratio of inductive reactance to resistance \((X/R\) ratio) of 2 . An uncompensated induction generator at rated output, typically, has a power factor of 0.89 leading, that is, \(P = - {2Q}\) . Thus, under these conditions, there is no apparent voltage rise in the circuit at full power. However, the real power loss \(\left( W\right)\) in the circuit is given approximately by:

\[ W = \left( {{P}^{2} + {Q}^{2}}\right) R/{V}_{0}^{2} \tag{A10.3} \]

The reactive power drawn by the generator acts to limit the voltage rise but higher real power losses are incurred in the connecting circuit.

Equations A10.1-A10.3 for voltage rise and circuit losses are approximate only and do not apply to heavily loaded circuits. A simple but precise calculation for voltage rise in any radial circuit may be carried out using an iterative technique.

Complex quantities are indicated by bold type.

At the generator busbar of Figure 10.9 the apparent power (sometimes known as the complex power) \({S}_{1}\) is given by:

\[ {\mathbf{S}}_{1} = P - {jQ} \tag{A10.4} \]

(for a generator operating at lagging power factor, exporting VArs, \({\mathbf{S}}_{\mathbf{1}}\) would be given by \(P + {jQ})\)

By definition \(\mathbf{S} = {\mathbf{{VI}}}^{ * }\) . * indicates the complex conjugate (i.e. the sign of the imaginary component of the complex number is reversed).

Therefore, the current flowing in the circuit is given by:

\[ \mathbf{I} = {\mathbf{S}}_{\mathbf{1}}^{ * }/{\mathbf{V}}_{\mathbf{1}}^{ * } = \left( {P + {jQ}}\right) /{\mathbf{V}}_{\mathbf{1}}^{ * } \tag{A10.5} \]

The voltage rise in the circuit is given by \(\mathbf{{IZ}}\) and so:

\[ {\mathbf{V}}_{\mathbf{1}} = {\mathbf{V}}_{\mathbf{0}} + \mathbf{{IZ}} = {\mathbf{V}}_{\mathbf{0}} + \left( {R + {jX}}\right) \left( {P + {jQ}}\right) /{\mathbf{V}}_{\mathbf{1}}^{ * } \tag{A10.6} \]

It is common for the network voltage \({\mathbf{V}}_{\mathbf{0}}\) to be defined and the generator busbar voltage \({\mathbf{V}}_{\mathbf{1}}\) required. \({\mathbf{V}}_{\mathbf{1}}\) can be obtained using the simple iterative expression:

\[ {\mathbf{V}}_{\mathbf{1}}^{\left( n + 1\right) } = {\mathbf{V}}_{\mathbf{0}} + \left( {R + {jX}}\right) \left( {P + {jQ}}\right) /{\mathbf{V}}_{\mathbf{1}}^{*\left( n\right) } \tag{10.7} \]

where \(n\) is the iteration number.

This is a simple form of the conventional Gauss-Seidel load flow algorithm (Weedy and Cory, 1998). Once the calculation converges an accurate solution is obtained. More complex load flow calculations may be carried out using commercially available power system analysis programs. These include models of transformers, with their tap changers, and can solve large interconnected circuits in only a few iterations using more advanced algorithms.

Example: Calculation of voltage rise in a radial circuit

Figure A10.2 Example of calculation of voltage rise on a radial circuit (all values in per unit)

Consider a 5 MW wind farm operating at a power factor of 0.98 leading. The network voltage \(\left( {\mathbf{V}}_{\mathbf{0}}\right)\) is \(\left( {1 + {j0}}\right)\) per unit and the circuit impedance \(\left( \mathbf{Z}\right)\) is \(\left( {{0.05} + {j0.1}}\right)\) per unit on a 10 MVA base (Figure A10.2).

A power factor of 0.98 leading implies a reactive power draw of 1.01 MVAr.

Thus, following Equation A10.7 the calculation becomes

\[ {\mathbf{V}}_{\mathbf{1}}^{\left( n + 1\right) } = 1 + \left( {{0.05} + {j0.1}}\right) \left( {{0.5} + {j0.101}}\right) /{\mathbf{V}}_{\mathbf{1}}^{*\left( n\right) } \]

For the first iteration \(\left( {n = 0}\right)\)

Assume

\[ {\mathbf{V}}_{\mathbf{1}}^{*\left( 0\right) } = 1 + {j0} \]

then \({\mathbf{V}}_{\mathbf{1}}^{\left( 1\right) }\) may be calculated to be:

\[ {\mathbf{V}}_{\mathbf{1}}^{\left( 1\right) } = {1.0149} + {j0.0551} \]

For the second iteration \(\left( {n = 1}\right)\)

\[ {\mathbf{V}}_{1}^{*\left( 1\right) } = {1.0149} - {j0.0551}\text{ then } \]
\[ {\mathbf{V}}_{1}^{\left( 2\right) } = {1.0117} + {j0.0549} \]

For the third iteration \(\left( {n = 2}\right)\)

\[ {\mathbf{V}}_{1}^{*\left( 2\right) } = {1.0117} - {j0.0.0549}\text{ then } \]
\[ {\mathbf{V}}_{1}^{\left( 3\right) } = {1.0117} + {j0.0551} \]

and the procedure has converged.

Therefore \({\mathbf{V}}_{1} = {1.013}\) per unit at an angle of \({3}^{ \circ }\) , that is, the voltage at the generator terminals is \({1.3}\%\) above that at the source. The angle between the two voltage vectors is small \(\left( {3}^{ \circ }\right)\) .

The approximate calculation \(\left( {{V}_{1} = {V}_{0} + \text{ PR-XQ }}\right)\) indicates a voltage \({V}_{1}\) of 1.015 per unit (i.e. a rise of 1.5%). This is confirmed by the results of the first iteration.

The current (I) in the circuit may be calculated from:

\[ \mathbf{I} = {\mathbf{S}}_{1}^{ * }/{\mathbf{V}}_{1}^{ * } = \left( {{0.5} + {j0.101}}\right) /\left( {{1.0117} - {j0.0551}}\right) \]
\[ = {0.4873} + {j0.1264}\text{ per unit } \]
\[ \left| \mathbf{I}\right| = {0.503}\text{ per unit } \]

With a connection voltage of \({33}\mathrm{{kV}}\) the base current is given by

\[ {I}_{\text{ base }} = V{A}_{\text{ base }}/\sqrt{}3 \times {V}_{\text{ base }} = 5 \times {10}^{6}/{1.732} \times {33} \times {10}^{3} = {87.5}\text{ Amps } \]

and so the magnitude of the current flowing in the \({33}\mathrm{{kV}}\) circuit is \({44}\mathrm{{Amps}}\) .

The real power loss in the circuit \(\left( W\right) {\text{ is }}^{3}\) :

\[ W = {I}^{2}R = {0.0127}\text{ per unit or }{127}\mathrm{\;{kW}} \]

The symmetrical short-circuit level at the generator busbar, before connection of the generators is simply:

\[ {S}^{\prime \prime } = 1/\left| \mathbf{Z}\right| = 1/{\left( {0.05}^{2} + {0.1}^{2}\right) }^{1/2} \]
\[ {S}^{\prime \prime } = {8.94}\mathrm{{pu}}\text{ or }{89.4}\mathrm{{MVA}} \]

Once the induction generators of a wind farm are connected then they will make a contribution to the short-circuit current seen by a circuit breaker when it closes on to a fault. This is typically some five times the rating of a directly connected fixed speed induction generator, for example some 25 MVA in this case, giving a total short-circuit level of 115 MVA. However, for a three-phase symmetrical fault the fault current contribution from an induction machine decays rapidly and will make only a small contribution to the fault current which must be interrupted by an opening circuit breaker. Detailed guidance on the calculation of fault currents, including the contribution from induction generators is given in IEC 60909.

\({}^{3}\) Note when the calculations are carried out using the per-unit system this is the aggregated power loss of all three phases.
